Medical Necessity Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved total knee arthroplasty (TKA) prosthesis is considered medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with ADLs from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee joint; and Limited range of motion, crepitus, or effusion or swelling of knee joint on physical examination: and Member has any of the following: Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis of knee joint (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix ); or Radiographic evidence of avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of tibial or femoral condyle; or Radiographic evidence or rheumatoid arthritis (joint space narrowing); and History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/body mass index (BMI)) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Footnote1 Note* ). content.content: {"url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0660.html?date=policy_history", "final_url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0660.html?date=policy_history", "http_status": 200, "content_type": "text/html", "login_wall": false, "blocked": false, "blocked_reason": null, "error": null, "text": "Knee Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna --> Top Knee Arthroplasty Clinical Policy Bulletins Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins Print Share Number: 0660 Table Of Contents Policy Applicable CPT / HCPCS / ICD-10 Codes Background References Policy Scope of Policy This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses knee arthroplasty. Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required. Medical Necessity Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved total knee arthroplasty (TKA) prosthesis is considered medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with ADLs from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee joint; and Limited range of motion, crepitus, or effusion or swelling of knee joint on physical examination: and Member has any of the following: Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis of knee joint (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix ); or Radiographic evidence of avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of tibial or femoral condyle; or Radiographic evidence or rheumatoid arthritis (joint space narrowing); and History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/body mass index (BMI)) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Footnote1 Note* ). Conservative therapy may be inappropriate for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint (medial and/or lateral but not patello-femoral) or severe angular deformity, or for avascular necrosis with collapse of tibial or femoral condyle, or progressive flexion contracture. If conservative therapy is not appropriate, the medical record must clearly document why such approach is not reasonable; or Failure of a previous osteotomy with pain interfering with ADLs; or Distal femur or proximal tibia malunion by imaging with pain interfering with ADLs; Distal femur or proximal tibia fracture or nonunion; or Malignancy of the distal femur, proximal tibia, knee joint or adjacent soft tissues by imaging; or Failure of previous unicompartmental knee replacement with pain interfering with ADLs. Footnote1 *Note: Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Members with osteoarthritis, traumatic arthritis, or avascular necrosis should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication) - with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year, including all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; and Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises; and Activity modification; and Supervised physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy; activities of daily living (ADLs) diminished despite completing a plan of care); and Assistive device use (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); and Therapeutic injections into the knee (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others). Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the knee; or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Vascular insufficiency, significant muscular atrophy of the leg, or neuromuscular disease severe enough to compromise implant stability or post-operative recovery or quadriplegia; or Osseous abnormalities that cannot be optimally managed and which would increase the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome (i.e., inadequate bone stock to support the implant); or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina). For members with significant conditions or co-morbidities, the risk/benefit of total knee arthroplasty should be appropriately addressed in the medical record. Footnote2 ** Relative contraindications to joint replacement include the following: morbid obesity (BMI greater than 40), age less than 50 years). Members with relative contraindications should exhaust all nonsurgical treatment options. Revision or replacement of total knee arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for the following indications when accompanied by pain and functional disability (interference with ADLs) (see also Additional Note ): Aseptic loosening of one or more prosthetic components confirmed by imaging; or Fracture of one or more components of the prosthesis or worn or dislocated plastic insert confirmed by imaging; or Confirmed periprosthetic infection by gram stain and culture (Note: A single stage revision is considered medically necessary for this indication, unless there has been a prior infection in the same joint, in which case a multi-stage revision may be considered medically necessary); or Periprosthetic fracture of distal femur, proximal tibia or patella confirmed by imaging; or Progressive or substantial periprosthetic bone loss confirmed by imaging; or Bearing surface wear leading to symptomatic synovitis; or Implant or knee malalignment (valgus/varus or flexion/extension greater than 15 degrees); or Knee arthrofibrosis; or Instability or dislocation of the TKA; or Extensor mechanism instability; And member does not have any of the following contraindications to total knee revision surgery: Poor bone quality; or Highly limited quadriceps or extensor function; or Poor skin coverage; or Poor vascular status.
